items.title: Enzymes don't 'fit' substrates — they fit transition states
items.claim: The textbook 'lock and key' model says enzymes have an active site that matches the substrate. Real enzymes are much more interesting: they bind the TRANSITION STATE of the reaction more tightly than the substrate or product.
items.prompt: Why does binding the transition state make a better catalyst?

options.text: It doesn't matter what the enzyme binds tightly
Stabilising the highest-energy point in the reaction lowers the activation energy; an enzyme that binds the transition state by 1000-fold relative to substrate accelerates the reaction by 1000-fold
Binding the substrate tightly always speeds up reactions
The substrate spontaneously becomes the transition state

items.reveal_title: Linus Pauling's prediction and modern enzyme design
items.reveal:
Pauling proposed in 1948 that enzymes catalyse reactions by binding most strongly to the transition state, lowering the activation energy.

Direct evidence: 'transition state analogues' — stable molecules that mimic the transition state's geometry — bind enzymes 10 to 10,000 times more tightly than the substrates themselves. Many drugs are designed this way (statins like atorvastatin mimic the transition state of HMG-CoA reductase).

Catalytic antibodies, raised against transition state analogues, can catalyse reactions for which no natural enzyme exists (Schultz, Lerner, 1986). De novo enzyme design (Baker lab, 2008 onward) explicitly engineers active sites to fit predicted transition states.

The induced-fit model (Koshland 1958) and the transition-state model are both refinements of the original lock-and-key.
items.why: Lock-and-key implies stable binding of stable molecules. Enzymes catalyse by binding unstable, fleeting transition states — a much subtler picture.

items.title: Your blood vessels stretched end to end would circle Earth twice
items.claim: The human body contains about 100,000 kilometres of blood vessels, almost all of which is capillaries. Earth's equator is 40,075 km. Two and a half wraps.
items.prompt: How is so much vessel length packed inside a person?

options.text: Capillaries are ~5-10 micrometres in diameter — they pass red blood cells in single file. Their tiny cross-section means enormous total length fits in tissue, while still leaving most tissue volume for cells
Vessels run in spirals to fit

items.reveal:
Aorta: ~2.5 cm diameter, 1 metre long. Branches into arteries, arterioles, then capillaries. Capillaries number ~10 billion in the body, total length ~80,000-100,000 km.

Almost every cell is within ~50 micrometres of a capillary — the maximum diffusion distance for oxygen. This drives the geometry: dense, thin, ramifying vessels.

Total cross-sectional area increases at each branching level: aorta ~5 cm^2, all capillaries combined ~4000 cm^2. By the conservation equation (flow = velocity * area), blood velocity drops from ~30 cm/s in the aorta to ~0.1 cm/s in capillaries — allowing time for diffusion.

Vascular networks follow allometric scaling laws (West, Brown, Enquist) that approximate optimal transport — minimising energy cost of moving blood. The same scaling rules describe trees, river networks, urban roads.

New capillary formation (angiogenesis) is closely controlled. Tumours hijack it to grow blood supply; anti-angiogenic drugs (bevacizumab) starve them.
items.why: A circulatory system 100,000 km long sounds external. It's packed inside a human body because each capillary is a fraction of a hair wide — and there are billions of them.

items.title: You are outnumbered by your own bacteria
items.claim: Adult humans carry about 38 trillion bacterial cells, roughly matching the count of human cells. By gene count, microbial DNA dwarfs human DNA by 100 to 1. They digest your food, train your immune system and affect your behaviour.

options.text: Humans have 10 times more bacteria than human cells
The ratio is closer to 1.3:1 (bacteria:human), based on revised counts (Sender, Fuchs & Milo 2016) — much closer than the older 10:1 figure suggested
There are about as many bacterial cells as human red blood cells
Bacterial cell count is roughly the same as human muscle cell count

items.reveal:
The famous 10:1 ratio came from a 1972 back-of-envelope estimate by Thomas Luckey. It propagated through textbooks for 40 years.

In 2016, Sender, Fuchs and Milo revisited the numbers. They estimated about 30 trillion human cells (84 percent red blood cells) and 38 trillion bacterial cells (most in the colon). The ratio is close to 1:1.

Gene count is a different story. Each human cell carries 20,000 genes; the gut microbiome contains an estimated 2 to 20 million unique microbial genes — so by gene count, we're 99 percent microbe.

The gut microbiome makes vitamins, ferments fibre, modulates the immune system and produces neurotransmitters that may affect mood and behaviour (the 'gut-brain axis').
items.why: Self/other has clear boundaries in popular imagination. Biologically, the boundary is fuzzy and statistical.
